prompt.context: Your client designs, manufactures and markets a full line of bicycles. The company had been growing in sales and profits when its profitability flattened, and then began declining 3 years ago.
prompt.question: What is causing the decline in profitability, and what would you recommend the client do to address it?

clarifying_info.a: Revenues are growing at roughly the same rate as before the downturn.

clarifying_info.q: Are both operating and administrative costs increasing?
clarifying_info.a: Administrative costs are growing, but operating costs appear to account for the bulk of increased expenses.

clarifying_info.q: Is the problem in fixed or variable costs?
clarifying_info.a: Fixed costs are growing but variable costs appear to account for the bulk of the increased expenses.

clarifying_info.q: What is driving the increase in variable costs?
clarifying_info.a: Both direct and indirect variable costs have been growing. Bicycles have become more sophisticated with better materials and components, but the increasing cost per bike has been comparable to the growing price/revenue per bike. Indirect costs are increasing disproportionately.

clarifying_info.q: What components of indirect variable cost are the issue — materials or labor?
clarifying_info.a: Allocations of indirect material are about the same (loss of bikes about the same). The allocation of indirect labor appears to be the big problem.

clarifying_info.q: Why is indirect labor increasing? What does WIP look like?
clarifying_info.a: WIP is increasing. On the factory floor, many bikes are waiting around. The bottlenecks are not capacity related — there is plenty of throughput available. Much time is being spent on set-up: resetting paint booths, welding jigs, dies and presses, etc.

clarifying_info.q: Has set-up time per run increased?
clarifying_info.a: No. Set-up time has actually decreased as the workforce has improved set-up tools and jigs.

clarifying_info.q: Has the number of set-ups increased?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the number of set-ups has increased.

framework: Diagnose profit decline: revenues vs. expenses
Break down expenses: operating vs. administrative
Break down operating costs: fixed vs. variable
Break down variable costs: direct vs. indirect
Break down indirect costs: materials vs. labor
Investigate indirect labor: examine WIP, factory floor, bottlenecks
Identify root cause: number of set-ups vs. set-up time per run
Link to strategic context: product line proliferation driven by industry specialization trend

questions.prompt: Is the revenue side or the cost side driving declining profitability?
questions.guidance: The candidate should structure a P&L-level diagnosis. Revenues are growing at a normal rate, so the issue is on the cost side. This narrows the investigation to expenses.

questions.prompt: Within costs, where is the problem — operating or administrative?
questions.guidance: The candidate should distinguish operating from administrative/overhead costs. Administrative costs are growing but the bulk of the increase is in operating costs.

questions.prompt: Within operating costs, is the problem in fixed or variable costs?
questions.guidance: Fixed costs are growing but variable costs are the primary driver of the increase. The candidate should articulate that variable costs scale with output, making them especially significant for a growing company.

questions.prompt: Within variable costs, is the problem in direct or indirect costs?
questions.guidance: Both have grown, but the key insight is that direct costs (better materials/components) have risen proportionally with revenue/price per bike and therefore are not the root cause. Indirect costs are increasing disproportionately.

questions.prompt: Within indirect variable costs, is the problem in materials or labor?
questions.guidance: Indirect material allocations are stable (loss rates are consistent). Indirect labor is the outlier and is growing disproportionately.

questions.prompt: Why is indirect labor increasing? What does the factory floor reveal?
questions.guidance: The candidate should investigate WIP levels and factory floor observations. WIP is rising and bikes are queuing — a symptom of bottlenecks. The bottleneck is not capacity but set-up time: resetting paint booths, welding jigs, dies, and presses.

questions.prompt: Is the set-up issue driven by longer set-up times or more frequent set-ups?
questions.guidance: The candidate must differentiate these two causes. Set-up time per run has actually decreased (workforce improvements to tools/jigs). Therefore the root cause is an increase in the number of set-ups, implying smaller batch sizes or more model variants.

brainstorming.prompt: The industry has been trending toward increased bicycle specialization (touring, mountain, racing, hybrid, etc.). What has the company done in response, and what solutions would address the root cause?

categories.name: Root Cause
ideas: Company responded to specialization trend by rapidly proliferating product lines
More SKUs means more production changeovers (set-ups) per period
Smaller batch sizes per model reduce economies of scale in assembly
Higher indirect labor from set-up time is not offset by price increases

categories.name: Product Line Rationalization
ideas: Eliminate low-volume or low-margin bicycle models
Focus on a defensible set of categories rather than full-line coverage
Use market data to identify which segments justify dedicated production runs

categories.name: Shared Components Strategy
ideas: Increase the number of components shared across model lines to reduce variety
Design a common frame or component platform for related models
Reduce the number of unique parts requiring distinct tooling set-ups

categories.name: Manufacturing Process
ideas: Group similar models into production families to batch set-ups
Invest in flexible tooling/jigs that can handle multiple models with minimal changeover
Apply lean manufacturing / SMED principles to minimize changeover time

recommendation: Rationalize the product line by eliminating or consolidating low-volume models that drive excessive set-ups without proportional revenue contribution
Redesign the product architecture to maximize shared components across model lines, reducing the number of unique set-ups required
risks: Cutting models may cede certain market segments to competitors
Customers accustomed to broad selection may switch brands
Shared-component design requires upfront R&D investment and product redesign cycles
next_steps: Conduct SKU-level profitability analysis to identify which models generate positive contribution after allocating indirect labor
Model the impact of component sharing on set-up frequency and indirect labor cost
Develop a product roadmap with rationalized line and phased transition plan
